title: Next Greater Element I
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning per query versus a single monotonic decreasing stack pass that resolves every value at once.

blocks.text: You are given two DISTINCT-valued arrays, nums1 and nums2, where nums1 is a subset of nums2. For each value in nums1, find its NEXT GREATER element in nums2: the first value to its right in nums2 that is strictly larger, or -1 if none exists.

blocks.caption: A single monotonic decreasing stack pass over nums2 resolves every value's next greater element in one linear scan

blocks.text: For every value queried (from nums1), its "next greater element" is defined entirely by its position and surroundings WITHIN nums2, not nums1; nums1 is really just a list of which answers to report.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Next Taller Person in a Line, for a Selected Few
blocks.text: Imagine a long line of people of different heights (nums2), and being asked: for a SPECIFIC selected few of them (nums1), who is the next taller person standing somewhere further down the line? A clever way to answer this for everyone at once (not just the selected few) is to walk down the line, keeping a stack of people who are still "waiting" to find someone taller ahead of them; the moment a taller person appears, they resolve the answer for everyone shorter currently waiting.

blocks.caption: The stack holds values still waiting for a bigger value to appear; a new bigger arrival resolves the answer for everyone smaller on top

blocks.text: Before scanning rightward from scratch for EACH queried value (redundant work, since nums2 does not change), notice that a SINGLE pass over nums2 using a monotonic stack resolves the next greater element for EVERY value in nums2 simultaneously.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The "next greater element" question, asked repeatedly for different starting positions in the SAME array, is a classic sign of the monotonic stack technique.

Observation 2: Walking through nums2 left to right, maintaining a stack of values still WAITING to find something greater than themselves further along: whenever a new value arrives that is bigger than the stack's current top, that new value IS the answer for the top (and possibly several more values below it, if they are also smaller).

Observation 3: Repeatedly popping and resolving while the stack's top is smaller than the new value correctly handles resolving MULTIPLE waiting values with a single new arrival.

Observation 4: Anything still left on the stack once the entire array has been scanned has no next greater element at all, so those get the default answer of -1.

Observation 5: Since nums1 is just a subset of nums2, solving for ALL of nums2 first (storing results in a hash map) and then looking up nums1's specific values afterward avoids ever needing to treat nums1 specially during the main algorithm.
This is the classic monotonic decreasing stack technique: solve "next greater element" for every value in nums2 in one linear pass, then simply look up the answers nums1 asks for.
For each value in nums1, find its exact position in nums2, then scan rightward from there for the first strictly larger value.

items: For each value x in nums1, locate its index in nums2.
Scan every position after that index, returning the first value strictly greater than x, or -1 if none is found.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Locating each value's exact index first is necessary, since the "next greater" search must start strictly AFTER that specific position.
The inner scan directly implements the definition of "next greater element" for one specific starting position.

blocks.text: Correctly finds each value's next greater element, since it directly scans exactly as the definition requires.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m*n), where m = nums1.length and n = nums2.length: for each of the m queries, an O(n) search (find index) plus an O(n) scan.
Space: O(1) extra (excluding the output).

Limitation: repeating a full rightward scan for every queried value is wasteful, since nums2 itself never changes; a single monotonic stack pass over nums2 resolves ALL next-greater answers simultaneously.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force redundantly rescans nums2 for every query. Instead, walk through nums2 ONCE, maintaining a monotonic decreasing stack of values still waiting for their next greater element. Whenever a new value is bigger than the stack's top, pop and record that new value as the answer for everything smaller on top, repeating until the stack's top is no longer smaller (or the stack is empty). After processing all of nums2, simply look up each value nums1 asks about in the resulting map (defaulting to -1 if never resolved).

Walk through nums2 with a stack. For each new value: while the stack is non-empty and its top is smaller than the new value, pop it and record the new value as its next-greater answer in a hash map. Push the new value. After the full walk, map each value in nums1 through the resulting hash map, defaulting to -1 for any value left unresolved.
Use a monotonic decreasing stack over nums2 to resolve every value's next greater element in one linear pass, then look up nums1's queries.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Looking up nums1 = [4,1,2] in the resolved map gives [-1,3,-1], matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n): each element of nums2 is pushed and popped at most once (O(n) total), plus O(m) for the final nums1 lookups.
Space: O(n), for the stack and the hash map in the worst case.

Each value pushed onto the stack represents "a value still waiting to find something bigger further to its right." The moment a bigger value arrives, it is guaranteed to be the FIRST (nearest) bigger value for every smaller value currently sitting on top of the stack (since anything even bigger would have already resolved them earlier). Popping and resolving repeatedly correctly handles a new arrival resolving multiple waiting values at once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A new value is bigger than the stack's top","Pop and resolve, possibly repeating for multiple smaller values below it"],["A new value is smaller than (or equal to) the stack's top","Simply pushed, joining the \"waiting\" values"],["Values remain on the stack after the full scan","They never found a next greater element, so they resolve to -1"]]}

items: The stack only ever holds values in DECREASING order from bottom to top, which is what makes the "pop while smaller" logic correct and efficient.
A hash map (rather than directly modifying nums1) decouples solving for all of nums2 from the specific subset nums1 happens to ask about.
The final list comprehension/loop simply looks up each nums1 value, defaulting to -1 for anything never resolved (left on the stack).

blocks.text: "Next greater element to the right," asked for many positions in the SAME array, is the defining signal for a monotonic decreasing stack: a single linear pass resolves every position's answer simultaneously, rather than repeating a scan per query.

items: Rescanning nums2 separately for each value in nums1, missing the opportunity to solve for ALL of nums2 in a single combined pass.
Popping only once per new value instead of repeatedly (in a while loop), which would fail to resolve multiple waiting smaller values at once.
Forgetting the default -1 for values left on the stack at the very end.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["nums2 is in strictly decreasing order","Every value ends up with -1, since nothing bigger ever appears further right"],["nums2 is in strictly increasing order","Every value (except the last) resolves immediately, since each new value is bigger than everything currently waiting"],["nums1 equals nums2 exactly","Every value in nums1 gets a genuinely resolved (or -1) answer, no different from the general case"]]}

items: Explicitly stating "solve for ALL of nums2 first, since nums1 is just a filter" up front avoids the common trap of treating nums1 as something requiring special handling during the main algorithm.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Next greater/smaller element to the right" (for one or many queried positions) points directly to the monotonic stack technique.

items: How would you find the next SMALLER element instead? Use a monotonic INCREASING stack instead, popping while the top is LARGER than the new value.

How would you handle a CIRCULAR array (as in Next Greater Element II elsewhere in this category)? Conceptually iterate over the array twice (or use modular indexing), letting values wrap around to search the beginning again.

What is the amortized cost per element, and why? O(1) amortized, since each element is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the entire algorithm, despite the appearance of a nested while loop.
The foundational monotonic stack pattern, directly extended (with circular wraparound) in Next Greater Element II and Next Greater Node in Linked List elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(m*n) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic stack, single pass): O(m + n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack for "next greater element"
Core Idea: Solve for every value in nums2 simultaneously using a single stack pass; a new bigger arrival resolves the answer for every smaller value currently waiting on the stack
Time: O(m + n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: nums1 is just a subset/filter; solving fully for nums2 first and looking up afterward avoids any redundant per-query work
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Monotonic decreasing stack; a bigger arrival resolves every smaller value waiting on top
